result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [DataScan.load_from_json()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Load a DataScan from a JSON file produced by save\_to\_json(). twitter-card: title: >- [DataScan.load_from_json()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Load a DataScan from a JSON file produced by save\_to\_json(). title: >- [DataScan.load_from_json()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Load a DataScan from a JSON file produced by save\_to\_json(). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Load a `DataScan` from a JSON file produced by `save_to_json()`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/datascan.py#L1051-L1121){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature DataScan.load_from_json(input_file) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} This is how a saved baseline is brought back: load the profile from the file, then pass it to the [`compare()`](`pointblank.DataScan.compare`) method of a new scan to find out what has changed since. The file is the one written by [`save_to_json()`](`pointblank.DataScan.save_to_json`) (or any file containing the output of [`to_json()`](`pointblank.DataScan.to_json`)). As with [`from_dict()`](`pointblank.DataScan.from_dict`), the loaded scan has the statistics but not the data, so drift scores are only computed for its Boolean columns. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [input_file]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The path to the JSON file. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [DataScan]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A restored `DataScan` instance. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Let's save a profile of a table of orders as a baseline. ::: {#eb23eee2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import polars as pl import tempfile from pathlib import Path orders = pl.DataFrame( {"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "amount": [25.0, 40.0, 15.5, 60.0]} ) baseline_path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "orders_profile.json" pb.DataScan(orders, tbl_name="orders").save_to_json(baseline_path) ``` ::: Later, the table has grown and a refund (a negative amount) has appeared. The baseline is loaded from the file and compared with a scan of the current table: ::: {#d56e7ed4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} orders_now = pl.DataFrame( {"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "amount": [25.0, 40.0, 15.5, 60.0, -15.5]} ) baseline = pb.DataScan.load_from_json(baseline_path) diff = pb.DataScan(orders_now, tbl_name="orders").compare(baseline) diff.to_dict()["stat_diffs"]["amount"]["min"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'baseline': 15.5, 'current': -15.5} ``` ::: ::: The minimum `amount` went from 15.5 to -15.5. A change like this is easy to miss in the data but stands out in a comparison of profiles, and a check such as [`Validate.col_vals_ge()`](`pointblank.Validate.col_vals_ge`) can then guard against it.
